overview: FAM4303 is a flight event focused on hard landings. The notes below are organized off the canonical syllabus items first, then filled out with local FAM gouge so students can brief the event, explain the why behind each item, and stay ahead of instructor follow-up questions.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

children.text: Hard Landings is judged by how well you enter it, stay ahead of the aircraft, and recover without needing cleanup coaching.
Setup / entry
Common Causes:
High Flare
Flare started too early or with excessive pitch-up
Can lead to stalling or nose gear striking runway during pitch correction
Late/Rapid Flare
Misjudged altitude or high descent rate
Can cause abrupt pitch-up → hard landing or approach-to-stall
Low Airspeed on Final
Exacerbated by idle power or delayed waveoff
High Sink Rate / Low Power on Final
May exceed safe touchdown parameters
Abrupt Control Movements
Final airspeed <110 KIAS increases risk of stall and hard touchdown
Idle or low power (<4-6%) on final + LDG flaps = rapid airspeed decay and high descent rate
Common errors / grading traps
The usual trap is missing the setup picture, then trying to salvage Hard Landings late.
Overview:

This procedure is used when the landing gear fails to indicate fully up with the gear handle up or fully down with the gear handle down. It’s applicable in situations involving abnormal gear or inboard door positions, and should be used to troubleshoot and determine whether gear indications are safe or if further emergency procedures are required.

Used when any landing gear is confirmed unsafe. A gear-up landing on a suitable area is preferred. Fly a flat, power-on, straight-in approach maintaining directional control with rudder. Treat any gear not fully extended as retracted.

Used to extend and lock the landing gear when normal extension fails or is impossible, typically directed by other emergency checklists. Once the emergency handle is pulled, landing gear and flap retraction are no longer possible.
High Temperature / High Pressure Altitude Conditions
(N) Execute this checklist anytime the gear doesn’t indicate fully up or down as expected.
LAMP test switch – Check

LDGGR CONT (left front console), INST (left front console), and INST LT (left rear console) circuit breakers – Check in/reset (If unable to reset the LDGGR CONT circuit breaker, execute the Emergency Gear Extension Checklist)
(N) “Reset” means to re-engage a circuit breaker that has tripped. Pilots should evaluate emergency severity and system losses before resetting or opening any circuit breaker.
Gear handle – Cycle
(N) Multiple gear handle cycles are allowed until fuel becomes critical or the PIC determines further attempts risk more damage or hydraulic pressure loss.
Actions that may help extend the gear during cycling include:
Applying side loads (slipping)
Using speed brake
(N) Prefer another aircraft’s visual inspection for abnormal gear/door positions. Don’t rush—coordinate when time permits.
(N) If only the nose gear is unsafe but main gear is down with doors closed, the down lock microswitch might be faulty. Resetting the LDGGR CONT CB may resolve it.
Gear handle – DOWN (Press down firmly. If unable to lower the gear handle, execute the Landing Gear Emergency Extension checklist) (BOTH)
(N) Confirm all position lights illuminate. Lamp test will not illuminate gear lights if the LDGGR CONT CB is tripped.

(C) If the LDGGR CONT circuit breaker trips, position indicator lights and gear handle lights will not work. Landing light, taxi light, and AOA indexers also become inoperative, preventing internal confirmation of "down and locked" gear.

(N) A tripped LDGGR CONT circuit breaker disables landing light, taxi light, and AOA indexers. If the INST circuit breaker trips in either cockpit, position indicator lights and gear handle lights in that cockpit become inoperative.

Note:

Asymmetric (split-flap) condition may cause uncommanded roll or yaw during flap operation. It results from either binding of flap segments or torque link failure between inner and outer flaps. Control authority is sufficient at pattern airspeeds.
Airspeed – Adjust to maintain control and minimize effort
Flap control handle – Move to minimize/eliminate asymmetry
(W) Once asymmetry is minimized or eliminated, do not reposition flap control handle.
Land – Use straight-in approach

Asymmetric (split-flap) condition may cause uncommanded roll or yaw during flap operation. It results from either binding of flap segments or torque link failure between inner and outer flaps. Control authority is sufficient at pattern airspeeds.
(N) Do not attempt to extend speed brake when experiencing asymmetric flaps
(N) If necessary, confirm flap position with tower flyby and/or visual inspection by another aircraft.
Controllability check – As required
